cards.q: Can directives have direct effect between private parties (horizontal direct effect)? Give the reasons for the Court of Justice's position and explain the ways around it. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. A directive cannot of itself impose obligations on an individual, so it cannot be relied on as such against a private party (Marshall I, Faccini Dori). There are no exceptions to this rule, only workarounds.
• Rule: a directive is binding, as to the result, only "upon each Member State to which it is addressed" (Art 288(3) TFEU). Its direct effect is therefore only vertical: a clear, precise and unconditional provision can be invoked against the state after the deadline where transposition is missing, faulty or not applied in practice (Ratti, 148/78; estoppel). Marshall I (152/84) excluded horizontal effect. Faccini Dori (C-91/92, a contract concluded at a railway station with a private company), Wells (C-201/02), Dominguez (C-282/10) and Smith (C-122/17: in a private dispute the court need not disapply contrary national law on the basis of the directive alone) confirm it. Contrast: Treaty provisions (Defrenne II, Art 157 TFEU; Angonese, Art 45 TFEU) and regulations (Muñoz, C-253/00) can bind private parties.
• Reasons: (1) directives are addressed only to Member States; (2) the private party has committed no default, so the estoppel argument does not reach it; (3) it would erase the distinction between directives and regulations, because the Union may impose obligations on individuals with immediate effect only where it is empowered to adopt regulations (Faccini Dori); (4) legal certainty: a private party cannot be expected to know that an untransposed directive binds it.
• Workarounds, roughly from safest to most adventurous: (1) a broad notion of the state: the state in any capacity, e.g. as employer (Marshall I), and emanations of the state (Foster, C-188/89; Farrell, C-413/15); (2) consistent interpretation, i.e. "indirect effect" (Von Colson, 14/83; Marleasing, C-106/89), never contra legem; (3) triangular situations and incidental effect (Wells; unnotified technical rules: CIA Security, C-194/94; Unilever, C-443/98); (4) a directive giving expression to a general principle or Charter right that works horizontally (Mangold, C-144/04; Kücükdeveci, C-555/07; Art 47 Charter in conjunction with Directive 1999/70, KL, C-715/20); (5) benefits under a regulation made conditional on compliance with a directive (Viamex Agrar, C-37/06 and C-58/06).
• Last resort: damages from the defaulting Member State before the national courts (Francovich). Non-transposition is per se a sufficiently serious breach (Dillenkofer, C-178/94).
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU, Art 47 Charter · Cases: Ratti (148/78), Marshall I (152/84), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Wells (C-201/02), Dominguez (C-282/10), Smith (C-122/17), Defrenne II (43/75), Angonese (C-281/98), Muñoz (C-253/00), Foster (C-188/89), Farrell (C-413/15), Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), CIA Security (C-194/94), Unilever (C-443/98), Mangold (C-144/04), Kücükdeveci (C-555/07), KL (C-715/20), Viamex Agrar (C-37/06 and C-58/06), Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90), Dillenkofer (C-178/94).

cards.q: What is meant by the "indirect effect" of directives? Explain its legal basis, its scope and its limits. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Indirect effect is the duty of all national authorities, above all the courts, to interpret national law as far as possible in the light of the wording and purpose of a directive (Von Colson, Marleasing). The directive is not applied itself but works through national law, so it reaches even disputes between private parties, but it never requires a contra legem reading.
• Basis: in Von Colson (14/83) the Court held that the Member States' obligation to achieve the directive's result (Art 288(3) TFEU) and the duty of sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU) bind all state authorities, including the courts within their jurisdiction. Effet utile supports this. The effect is "indirect" because the court applies national law read in conformity with the directive. Unlike direct effect, the directive's provision need NOT be clear, precise and unconditional.
• Scope: all national law, whether adopted before or after the directive (Marleasing, C-106/89), and also in horizontal disputes. That makes it the main workaround for the lack of horizontal direct effect. The court must consider the whole body of national law and use every interpretative method national law recognises (Pfeiffer, C-397/01 to C-403/01), if necessary departing from settled national case law (DI, C-441/14). The duty applies to EU law generally, not only to directives. Timing: from the end of the transposition period; before that, courts must refrain from interpretations that would seriously compromise the directive's objective (Adeneler, C-212/04).
• Limits: only "as far as possible", so never contra legem (Adeneler; Dominguez, C-282/10). It is bounded by legal certainty and non-retroactivity, and it can never determine or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis, 80/86; Pupino, C-105/03). A common wrong answer says courts must read national law contra legem "if the national system allows it". In fact EU law obliges them to exhaust every interpretative method their own law recognises, and the duty ends where a conforming reading would be contra legem.
• Where a conforming reading is impossible: another workaround (a general principle or Charter right, incidental effect) or a state liability claim (Francovich).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU, Art 288(3) TFEU · Cases: Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Pfeiffer (C-397/01 to C-403/01), DI (C-441/14), Adeneler (C-212/04), Dominguez (C-282/10), Kolpinghuis (80/86), Pupino (C-105/03), Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Under the ordinary legislative procedure the Council is negotiating (1) a regulation under Art 48 TFEU on the aggregation of social-security periods for migrant workers and (2) a directive under Art 83(1) TFEU laying down minimum rules on the definition of computer crime and its penalties. The minister of Member State Lusitania declares that (1) would affect the financial balance of its pension system; the minister of Member State Dacia considers that (2) would affect fundamental aspects of its criminal justice system. (a) What can each of them do, and what happens to the procedure? (b) In the European Council there is no consensus on (2), but ten Member States want to go ahead. What follows? (c) What does 'reverse qualified majority voting' mean, and where is it used? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both can pull the 'emergency brake': the draft goes to the European Council and the OLP is suspended; draft (1) dies unless the European Council sends it back within four months, while for draft (2) ten states can proceed by enhanced cooperation, which is deemed authorised; reverse QMV means a Commission proposal stands unless a qualified majority rejects it.
• Function: a political safety valve for sensitive fields that Lisbon moved to QMV/OLP. One Council member can halt the procedure and the European Council decides, by consensus (Art 15(4) TEU). For social security this works as a de facto veto, because sending the draft back needs consensus; for criminal law the others can still go ahead by enhanced cooperation.
• (a)(1) Social security, Art 48 second subpara TFEU: a member declares that the draft would affect important aspects of its social security system (scope, cost, financial structure) or its financial balance; the matter is referred to the European Council and the OLP is suspended. Within four months the European Council either refers the draft back to the Council (the OLP continues) or takes no action or requests a new Commission proposal – then the act originally proposed is deemed not adopted.
• (a)(2) Criminal law, Art 83(3) TFEU (parallel rule for criminal procedure in Art 82(3)): a member considering that the draft would affect fundamental aspects of its criminal justice system may request referral; the OLP is suspended; in case of consensus the European Council refers the draft back within four months and the OLP resumes.
• (b) Within the same four months, in case of disagreement, if at least nine Member States wish to establish enhanced cooperation on the basis of the draft, they notify the EP, the Council and the Commission, and the authorisation under Art 20(2) TEU and Art 329(1) TFEU is deemed granted. Ten states suffice; Dacia and the others are not bound. Art 48 TFEU has no such fast-track.
• (c) Reverse QMV: a Commission recommendation is deemed adopted unless the Council rejects it by QMV within a short deadline – the burden is inverted and the Commission strengthened. It is not in the Treaty text: Art 126 TFEU uses ordinary QMV without the vote of the state concerned (Art 126(13)); reverse QMV was added for euro-area sanctions in the excessive deficit procedure by the Six-Pack (Reg 1173/2011) and by Art 7 of the Fiscal Compact (TSCG).
Codex: Art 15(4), 20(2) TEU; Art 48, 82(3), 83(1)–(3), 126(13), 329(1) TFEU (the brake for substantive criminal law is in Art 83(3), not 83(2)) · Reg 1173/2011 and Art 7 TSCG (not in codex).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: The government of Member State Aurelia proposes amending the Treaties so that the Union obtains a shared competence to regulate the organisation and financing of national hospital systems. (a) Which revision procedure must be used, and who may initiate it? (b) Describe the steps until entry into force, including the role of a Convention. (c) Could the European Council instead use the simplified revision procedure of Art 48(6) TEU? (d) Two years after signature 22 of the 27 Member States have ratified the amending treaty, but a referendum in Borvania has failed. Does the treaty enter into force for the 22? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only the ordinary revision procedure (Art 48(2)–(5) TEU) can confer a new competence; the simplified procedure is excluded because it may not increase the Union's competences; and the amendment cannot enter into force without ratification by all Member States – Art 48(5) merely sends the matter to the European Council.
• (a) Health is today mainly a supporting competence (Art 6(a), 168 TFEU; shared only for common safety concerns in public health, Art 4(2)(k)), and Art 168(7) reserves the organisation and delivery of health services to the Member States. Extending Union competence requires a Treaty amendment; Art 48(2) TEU expressly allows proposals that increase or reduce competences. Initiative: the government of any Member State, the EP or the Commission submits the proposal to the Council, which forwards it to the European Council; national parliaments are notified.
• (b) The European Council, after consulting the EP and the Commission (and the ECB for institutional changes in the monetary area), decides by simple majority to examine the amendments (Art 48(3)). Its President convenes a Convention of representatives of national parliaments, heads of state or government, the EP and the Commission, which adopts by consensus a recommendation to an intergovernmental conference. The European Council may, by simple majority and with the EP's consent, decide not to convene a Convention if the extent of the amendments does not justify it, and then sets the conference's mandate itself. The conference, convened by the President of the Council, determines the amendments by common accord; they enter into force after ratification by all Member States in accordance with their constitutional requirements (Art 48(4)).
• (c) No. Art 48(6) (unanimous European Council decision after consulting the EP and Commission, then approval by all Member States) covers only Part Three TFEU on internal policies and 'shall not increase the competences conferred on the Union'. It was used to insert Art 136(3) TFEU (ESM), upheld in Pringle (C-370/12).
• (d) No. Art 48(5): if after two years four fifths of the Member States (22 of 27 exceeds 21.6) have ratified and one or more have difficulties, the matter is referred to the European Council. This opens only a political discussion (in practice: guarantees for the state concerned and a second vote, as with the Irish referendums on Nice and Lisbon), not entry into force for the 22.
Codex: Art 48(2)–(6) TEU; Art 4(2)(k), 6(a), 136(3), 168(7) TFEU · Pringle (C-370/12).

cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. (a) 'Because of the principle of conferral, EU institutions may exercise only those powers that are expressly written in the Treaties.' (b) 'The principle of conferral concerns only the relationship between the Union and the Member States.' (c) 'The doctrine of implied powers and Art 352 TFEU are the same thing.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three are false: implied powers exist (Fédération Charbonnière); conferral also governs the horizontal distribution of powers among the institutions (Art 13(2) TEU); and implied powers attach to an existing express power, whereas Art 352 TFEU is a separate subsidiary legal basis with its own procedure.
• (a) False. Conferral (Art 1, 4(1), 5(1)–(2) TEU) means there is no general competence and every binding act needs a legal basis. But the Court recognises implied powers: the Union also has the powers without which the express provisions would have no meaning or could not reasonably and usefully be applied (Fédération Charbonnière de Belgique v High Authority, 8/55: fixing coal prices under the ECSC Treaty). Germany v Commission (281/85, migration policy): where an article confers a specific task on the Commission, it necessarily confers the powers indispensable to carry it out – there a binding decision on notification and consultation, but not a power to dictate the content of national policy. External counterpart: ERTA (22/70), today Art 3(2) and 216(1) TFEU.
• (b) False. Vertical distribution: Union v Member States – may the Union act at all (Art 5 TEU, Arts 2–6 TFEU)? Horizontal distribution: which institution may act, in which procedure (Art 13(2) TEU: each institution acts within the limits of its powers and in conformity with the procedures; institutional balance). An act can be annulled for either defect, e.g. wrong legal basis or procedure (lack of competence or infringement of an essential procedural requirement, Art 263(2) TFEU).
• (c) False. Implied powers stretch an express competence and follow its procedure. Art 352 TFEU is a written flexibility clause for cases where the Treaties have not provided the necessary powers to attain a Treaty objective: Council unanimity on a Commission proposal, EP consent, national parliaments alerted, no harmonisation where the Treaties exclude it, no CFSP objectives (Art 352(1)–(4)).
Codex: Art 1, 4(1), 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU; Art 2–6, 3(2), 216(1), 263(2), 352 TFEU · Fédération Charbonnière (8/55), Germany v Commission (281/85), ERTA (22/70).

cards.q: (a) Paula, a French national, enrols in a vocational hairdressing course at a public school in State Karolia. Karolian law requires non-nationals to pay an enrolment fee from which Karolian students are exempt. Paula relies directly on Art 18 TFEU. (b) Tom works for a private software company in Karolia and is dismissed because of his sexual orientation. Karolia has not transposed the relevant part of Directive 2000/78, although the deadline has passed. Tom relies directly on Art 19 TFEU against his employer. Assess both claims. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Paula can rely on Art 18 TFEU, a clear and unconditional prohibition with direct effect; Tom cannot rely on Art 19 TFEU, which is only a legislative competence, and must use other routes (Art 21(1) Charter, consistent interpretation, state liability).
• Test: a provision has direct effect if it is clear, precise and unconditional and confers rights (Van Gend en Loos, 26/62). Treaty articles can meet it; the wording decides.
• (a) Art 18(1) TFEU: 'within the scope of application of the Treaties ... any discrimination on grounds of nationality shall be prohibited' – a negative, unconditional prohibition needing no implementing measure (the legislative power in Art 18(2) does not make it conditional). Scope: access to vocational training falls within the Treaties (Gravier, 293/83: enrolment fee charged only to foreign students was discriminatory; today Art 166 TFEU). The fee is direct discrimination; Paula can invoke Art 18 against the public school, and the national rule must be disapplied.
• (b) Art 19(1) TFEU: the Council 'may take appropriate action to combat discrimination' based on sex, racial or ethnic origin, religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation, acting unanimously in a special legislative procedure with the EP's consent. It is a competence to legislate, not a prohibition, and gives individuals nothing to invoke – no direct effect.
• Tom's routes: the directive has no horizontal direct effect against a private employer (Faccini Dori, C-91/92), but national law must be read in conformity with it (Marleasing). Because the situation is governed by EU law (Directive 2000/78; Art 51(1) Charter), Art 21(1) Charter, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, is mandatory and can be invoked even between private parties (Egenberger, C-414/16; Mangold/Kücükdeveci line). Otherwise: a Francovich claim against Karolia.
Codex: Art 18, 19, 166, 288(3) TFEU; Art 21(1), 51(1) Charter · Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Gravier (293/83), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Egenberger (C-414/16), Mangold (C-144/04).

cards.q: Leonidas is a laboratory research scientist employed by the Austrian Ministry of Agriculture. Directive 2010/123 (fictitious) requires that laboratory research scientists be paid at least three times the normal hourly rate for weekend shifts; the implementation deadline was 31 December 2012. The Research Scientists Act 2000 (fictitious), which has never been amended, provides for only twice the normal hourly rate, and that is what Leonidas receives for his weekend shifts. Leaving aside any damages action against the Austrian state, does Leonidas have a cause of action against his employer under EU law? (6 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – the pay rule is unconditional and sufficiently precise, the deadline has passed, Austria has not implemented it correctly and the employer is the state itself, so Leonidas can rely on the directive vertically and claim three times the hourly rate; the conflicting Act must be disapplied.
• Starting point: a directive binds the Member State only as to the result (Art 288(3) TFEU); the rule is that directives have no direct effect. As an exception, individuals may rely on a directive against the state if the conditions of vertical direct effect are met (Van Duyn, 41/74; Ratti, 148/78).
• Consistent interpretation first (Von Colson, 14/83; Marleasing, C-106/89): the Act's clear figure 'twice' cannot be read as 'three times' without interpreting it contra legem, so direct effect is needed.
• (1) Deadline: 31 December 2012 has passed, so Austria can no longer rely on the transposition period (Ratti).
• (2) Implementation error: the Act of 2000 was never adapted and falls short of the directive's result – non-transposition or incorrect transposition. A pre-existing law counts as transposition only if it already guarantees the result.
• (3) Clear, precise, unconditional, conferring rights: the beneficiaries (laboratory research scientists), the debtor's obligation (pay) and the minimum content (at least three times the normal hourly rate for weekend shifts) can be read from the directive alone; no discretion or further measure is needed. The word 'at least' does not make it conditional; it only lets the state pay more.
• (4) Defendant = the state: the Ministry of Agriculture is part of the state administration, and the state can be sued in any capacity, including as employer (Marshall I, 152/84). No Foster/Farrell test is needed. Rationale: estoppel – the state may not profit from its own failure to implement.
• Consequence: the competent Austrian court or authority must disapply the 'twice' rule to the extent of the conflict (primacy, Simmenthal, 106/77) and apply the directive. Leonidas can claim the difference for his weekend shifts, subject to national procedural rules such as limitation periods, which must respect equivalence and effectiveness (Rewe, 33/76; Comet, 45/76).
• Contrast: had he worked for a private laboratory, the directive could not be invoked horizontally (Faccini Dori, C-91/92); only consistent interpretation, the workarounds, or state liability would remain.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Van Duyn (41/74), Ratti (148/78), Marshall I (152/84), Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Simmenthal (106/77), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Rewe (33/76).

cards.q: A Commission regulation on export refunds for live cattle provides that no refund is paid if the competent authority finds that the animal-welfare rules of a transport directive have not been complied with. The exporter Bovex, a private company, shipped cattle to Lebanon without the 24-hour rest period required by the directive, and the national customs office refuses the refund. Bovex argues that a directive can never impose obligations on individuals. Is Bovex right? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – the obligation does not come from the directive but from the regulation, which is directly applicable and makes the refund conditional on compliance with the directive (Viamex Agrar, C-37/06 and C-58/06).
• Rule: a directive cannot of itself impose obligations on an individual and cannot be relied on as such against him, whether by another private party (Marshall I, Faccini Dori) or by the state (no 'inverse' direct effect, Kolpinghuis, 80/86).
• Workaround: the refusal rests on the regulation, which is binding in its entirety and directly applicable (Art 288(2) TFEU) and incorporates the directive's standards as a condition for a benefit. The directive does not act on its own; it only supplies the content of the condition, and Bovex can obtain the refund only by meeting it.
• Result: the customs office may lawfully refuse the refund. In the lecture's list this is the fifth workaround – benefits under a regulation made conditional on compliance with a directive: the regulation supplies the binding force, the directive the content.
Codex: Art 288(2)–(3) TFEU · Viamex Agrar (C-37/06 and C-58/06), Kolpinghuis (80/86), Faccini Dori (C-91/92).

cards.q: Directive 1999/70, which gives effect to the social partners' framework agreement on fixed-term work, prohibits in clause 4 treating fixed-term workers less favourably than comparable permanent workers unless this is objectively justified. The labour code of State Polonia obliges employers to state in writing the reasons for terminating a permanent contract, but not a fixed-term contract. KL's private employer terminates his fixed-term contract with notice and gives no reasons, so KL cannot assess whether to challenge the dismissal. Can KL rely on EU law against his employer, and what must the national court do? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – the directive itself cannot be invoked against a private employer, but because the situation is governed by EU law, Art 47 Charter applies; Art 47 is sufficient in itself and can be invoked together with the directive, so the court must disapply the discriminatory provision if it cannot interpret national law consistently (KL, C-715/20, 2024).
• Substance: the difference in treatment concerns employment conditions and is not objectively justified, so clause 4 precludes the national rule (first part of the ruling).
• Obstacle: a private employer means no horizontal direct effect of a directive (Marshall I, 152/84; Faccini Dori, C-91/92). The court must first try a conforming interpretation (Marleasing), but not contra legem.
• Charter: in regulating the termination of fixed-term contracts the state implements the directive, so the Charter applies (Art 51(1)). Without reasons the fixed-term worker lacks the information needed to assess and challenge the dismissal – his access to a court is restricted, which infringes the right to an effective remedy (Art 47). Art 47 needs no concretisation by EU or national law and confers a right that individuals can invoke, also against private parties.
• Result: the national court must disapply the provision at issue (in the real case Art 30(4) of the Polish Labour Code) to the extent necessary to ensure the full effect of Art 47. This is the fourth workaround – a primary-law right does the horizontal work, as in Mangold and Egenberger, now with Art 47 Charter as the vehicle.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU; Art 47, 51(1) Charter; Directive 1999/70, clause 4 (not in codex) · KL (C-715/20), Egenberger (C-414/16), Faccini Dori (C-91/92).

cards.q: State Italica levied an additional excise surcharge on electricity, which its supreme court has since found contrary to a clear, precise and unconditional provision of Excise Directive 2008/118. Electricity suppliers paid the surcharge to the state and passed it on to their customers. Under national law a final consumer may recover sums unduly paid only in a civil action against its supplier, who may then claim a refund from the tax authority; there is no direct claim against the state. The textile producer Tessa sues its private supplier for repayment. (a) Can the court disapply the national tax provision in that action? (b) What follows if the action against the supplier therefore fails? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) In principle no, because a directive cannot be relied on against a private supplier – unless national law allows such disapplication or the supplier is an emanation of the state; (b) the principle of effectiveness then requires that Tessa can claim reimbursement directly from the state (Gabel Industria Tessile, C-316/22, 2024).
• (a) Art 288(3) TFEU: a directive cannot of itself impose obligations on a private party or be relied on as such against it, so in a dispute between private parties the court cannot disapply the national tax law on the basis of the directive alone. Two exceptions: (1) national law may itself empower courts to disapply national provisions contrary to EU law without direct effect – horizontal effect produced by national, not EU, law; (2) if the supplier is subject to the authority or control of the state or has special powers, it counts as the state (Foster, C-188/89; Farrell, C-413/15) – for the national court to check.
• (b) Procedural autonomy is limited by effectiveness: national rules must not make the exercise of EU rights practically impossible or excessively difficult (Rewe, 33/76; Impact, C-268/06). A consumer who bore an unlawful tax must be able to recover it from the supplier and, if that is impossible or excessively difficult, directly from the state. Here recovery from the supplier is legally impossible (no horizontal direct effect), so a system that allows claims only against the supplier infringes effectiveness, and the bar on a direct claim against the state must be set aside.
• In addition a state liability claim remains possible (Francovich); compare Thelen Technopark (C-261/20): no disapplication between private parties on the basis of a directive alone, but the injured party may claim damages from the state.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU; Art 4(3), 19(1) TEU · Gabel Industria Tessile (C-316/22), Thelen Technopark (C-261/20), Foster (C-188/89), Impact (C-268/06), Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90).

cards.q: In 2019 the agricultural authority of State Batavia classified poultry exports of Hendriks BV under a tariff heading carrying a lower export refund and demanded partial repayment. In 2021 the highest administrative court, against whose decisions there is no appeal, dismissed Hendriks's action, interpreting the Common Customs Tariff itself without making a preliminary reference. In 2025 the Court of Justice, in a case from another Member State, interprets the heading in Hendriks's favour. Hendriks learns of that judgment a week later and at once asks the authority to reopen its final decision. Must the authority do so? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, provided national law gives the authority power to reopen: under the duty of sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU) a final administrative decision must be reviewed where the four Kühne & Heitz conditions (C-453/00) are met, as they appear to be here.
• Principle: legal certainty – administrative decisions that have become final are in principle not reopened, and EU law does not generally require it, although interpretative rulings of the Court apply ex tunc.
• Kühne & Heitz (C-453/00): an administrative body must, on application, review a final decision to take account of a later interpretation by the Court where (1) national law gives it power to reopen the decision; (2) the decision became final as a result of a judgment of a court ruling at final instance; (3) that judgment, in the light of later CJEU case law, was based on a misinterpretation of EU law adopted without a reference under Art 267(3) TFEU; and (4) the person complained to the authority immediately after becoming aware of the Court's decision.
• Application: (2) and (3) are met – a court of last instance decided without the reference it was obliged to make; (4) is met – the application came within a week; (1) depends on national administrative procedure law, which must not treat EU-law errors less favourably than domestic ones (equivalence; compare i-21 Germany, C-392/04).
• Limits and alternatives: EU law does not require national courts to set aside their own final judgments (res judicata, Kapferer, C-234/04). Other routes: state liability for the supreme court's breach (Köbler, C-224/01) and infringement proceedings (Commission v France, C-416/17).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 267(3) TFEU · Kühne & Heitz (C-453/00), i-21 Germany (C-392/04), Kapferer (C-234/04), Köbler (C-224/01).

cards.q: The Austrian Verwaltungsgerichtshof refers questions on the interpretation of the General Data Protection Regulation to the Court of Justice in a dispute between a search-engine operator and the Austrian data protection authority. (a) Describe what happens to the national proceedings and to the reference until the Court of Justice gives judgment. (b) An Austrian NGO that is not a party to the national case, and the Irish government, want to put forward their views. May they? (c) Must there always be an oral hearing and an Opinion of the Advocate General? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The national court stays its proceedings; the Registrar notifies the participants listed in Art 23 of the Statute, who have two months for written observations; Ireland may take part as a Member State, the NGO only if the referring court admits it as a party; neither a hearing nor an AG Opinion is mandatory.
• (a) The referring court suspends its proceedings and sends the order for reference with the questions, facts, national law and reasons (Art 23 Statute; Art 94 RoP). The Registrar notifies the parties to the main proceedings, all Member States, the Commission and the institutions that adopted the act (here Parliament and Council); written observations are due within two months. A Judge-Rapporteur and an AG are designated (Arts 15, 16 RoP); the Judge-Rapporteur's preliminary report proposes the formation (chamber of three or five, Grand Chamber) and whether to dispense with a hearing or an Opinion (Art 59 RoP). Then come the hearing if any, the Opinion and the judgment, whose operative part answers the questions; the national court then resumes and decides the case.
• (b) Ireland: yes – every Member State may submit observations (Art 23 Statute, Art 96 RoP). NGO: the parties to the main proceedings are those determined by the referring court under national procedural rules (Art 97(1) RoP), so it can take part only if the VwGH admits it as a party or intervener – as NGOs were before the Conseil d'État in Google v CNIL (C-507/17). Intervention under Art 40 Statute concerns direct actions only (the lecture slide mentions Art 40, but in references participation rests on Art 23 Statute and Arts 96–97 RoP).
• (c) No. The Court may dispense with a hearing if it has sufficient information (Art 76(2)–(3) RoP) and with an AG Opinion if the case raises no new point of law (Art 20, last paragraph, Statute); it may rule by reasoned order if the question is identical to one already answered, clearly deducible from case law or free of reasonable doubt (Art 99 RoP), or if the reference is manifestly inadmissible (Art 53(2) RoP). Urgent (Art 107 RoP; persons in custody, Art 267(4) TFEU) and expedited (Art 105 RoP) procedures also exist.
Codex: Art 267 TFEU; Statute of the Court (Protocol No 3) Arts 20, 23, 40 · Rules of Procedure Arts 15, 16, 53, 59, 76, 94, 96, 97, 99, 105, 107 (not in codex) · Google v CNIL (C-507/17).

cards.q: Three situations in Member State Hungaria. (a) A first-instance court refers questions on freedom of establishment to the Court of Justice; under the national code of civil procedure the defendant appeals against the order for reference, and the appeal court sets the order aside and instructs the first-instance court to decide the case itself. (b) In another case, national law binds a lower court to the legal assessment of a higher court that has quashed its judgment; the lower court thinks that assessment is contrary to EU law. (c) In a third case, a party asks a first-instance court to make a reference and the court refuses. Assess each situation. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) The appeal court cannot remove the referring court's power to refer – the Court of Justice stays seised unless the referring court itself withdraws the reference (Cartesio); (b) the lower court may refer and must disregard guidance contrary to EU law (Rheinmühlen, Elchinov); (c) a first-instance court has discretion and the parties cannot compel a reference.
• Principle: Art 267(2) TFEU gives every court or tribunal an autonomous power to refer. Whether and what to refer is for the national court alone, and national rules cannot restrict that power (primacy of Art 267).
• (a) Cartesio (C-210/06): Art 267 does not rule out a national appeal against an order for reference as such, but the referring court's jurisdiction cannot be called into question by rules allowing an appeal court to vary or set aside the order and order the proceedings to resume. The Court of Justice remains seised as long as the referring court does not withdraw the reference (Art 100(1) RoP), so the first-instance court may maintain it.
• (b) Rheinmühlen (166/73): a rule binding a court on points of law to a superior court's rulings cannot deprive it of the power to refer. Elchinov (C-173/09): it must disregard instructions that conflict with EU law as interpreted by the Court. Judges may not face disciplinary proceedings for having made a reference (Miasto Łowicz, C-558/18 and C-563/18).
• (c) The parties may suggest a reference but have no right to one; a court whose decisions can be appealed may refer but need not (Art 267(2)), except where it considers an EU act invalid (Foto-Frost, 314/85). The duty to refer lies on the court of last instance (Art 267(3)), subject to the CILFIT exceptions.
Codex: Art 267(2)–(3) TFEU; Art 19(1) TEU · Cartesio (C-210/06), Rheinmühlen (166/73), Elchinov (C-173/09), Miasto Łowicz (C-558/18 and C-563/18), Foto-Frost (314/85), CILFIT (283/81); RoP Art 100 (not in codex).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: By a decision addressed to Austria, the Commission declares incompatible with the internal market an aid scheme that an Austrian Land had set up under its own legislative powers for regional ski-lift operators, and orders recovery. (a) The Land wants to bring an action for annulment as a 'Member State' under Art 263(2) TFEU. Can it? (b) Can it bring an action on another basis? (c) What other way is there to challenge the decision? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No – 'Member State' in Art 263(2) means only the central government; (b) yes, as a legal person under Art 263(4), and it is likely to be directly and individually concerned because the decision prevents it from exercising its own powers as it sees fit; (c) Austria itself may sue as a privileged applicant.
• (a) Privileged applicants are the Member States, the EP, the Council and the Commission (Art 263(2)). Regions, Länder and municipalities are not 'Member States' for the purposes of the institutional and judicial provisions, whatever their constitutional powers – otherwise the institutional balance would be upset (Région wallonne v Commission, C-95/97). The Committee of the Regions' semi-privileged standing (Art 263(3)) protects only its own prerogatives.
• (b) As a legal person under national law the Land is a non-privileged applicant (Art 263(4)). The decision is addressed to Austria, so it must show direct and individual concern. Direct: Austria has no discretion – it must recover the aid (Art 108(2) TFEU). Individual: the decision concerns aid granted by the Land itself under its own powers and prevents it from exercising them as it sees fit, which distinguishes it like an addressee (Vlaams Gewest v Commission, T-214/95). A general interest of a regional authority in the economy of its territory would not suffice. Forum: the General Court (Art 256(1)); time limit: two months (Art 263(6)).
• (c) Austria may bring the action as a privileged applicant without showing any interest – also before the General Court, because a Member State's action against a Commission state-aid decision is not reserved to the Court of Justice (Art 51 Statute). Alternatively, when recovery is enforced against the ski-lift operators, they can contest the decision's validity before a national court, which can refer under Art 267 – unless they could undoubtedly have brought an annulment action in time themselves (TWD, C-188/92).
Codex: Art 108(2), 256(1), 263(2)–(4), (6), 267 TFEU; Art 51 Statute · Région wallonne (C-95/97), Vlaams Gewest (T-214/95), Plaumann (25/62), TWD (C-188/92).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. (a) 'Like the ECHR, the Charter of Fundamental Rights protects only civil and political rights.' (b) 'Companies can invoke all Charter rights, including human dignity.' (c) 'Only citizens of the Union can rely on the Charter.' (d) 'The Charter extends the Union's competences to all fields of fundamental rights.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All four statements are false.
• (a) False. The Charter contains all three 'generations': civil and political rights (Titles I–III, V, VI: dignity, freedoms, equality, citizens' rights, justice); social rights (Title IV Solidarity, e.g. Art 27 information and consultation, Art 30 protection against unjustified dismissal, Art 31 fair working conditions, Art 34 social security); and collective rights (Art 37 environmental protection, Art 38 consumer protection). Many social provisions are 'principles' (Art 52(5)), which courts can use only to interpret and review implementing acts, not as free-standing rights (AMS, C-176/12, on Art 27).
• (b) False. Legal persons hold the rights that fit their nature – freedom to conduct a business (Art 16), property (Art 17), an effective remedy (Art 47; DEB, C-279/09) – but not highly personal rights such as human dignity (Art 1), the right to life (Art 2) or the prohibition of torture (Art 4).
• (c) False. Most rights belong to 'everyone'. Only some rights are reserved to Union citizens: the freedom to seek employment and work in any Member State (Art 15(2)), voting in EP and municipal elections (Arts 39, 40), free movement (Art 45(1)) and diplomatic and consular protection (Art 46). Access to documents, the Ombudsman and petitions also extend to residents and legal persons registered in a Member State (Arts 42–44).
• (d) False. The Charter binds the Union's institutions always and the Member States only when they implement Union law (Art 51(1); Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10: within the scope of EU law). It does not extend the field of application of Union law or create new powers (Art 51(2); Art 6(1) second subpara TEU).
Codex: Art 6(1) TEU; Charter Arts 1, 2, 4, 15(2), 16, 17, 27–38, 39–46, 47, 51, 52(5) · AMS (C-176/12), DEB (C-279/09), Åkerberg Fransson (C-617/10).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. (a) 'MEPs sit in national delegations and must vote as their political group decides.' (b) 'Twenty MEPs from five Member States may form a political group.' (c) 'An Austrian MEP may at the same time remain a member of the Austrian Nationalrat.' (d) 'The European Parliament may decide by a majority of its members to hold all its plenary sessions in Brussels.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All four statements are false.
• (a) False. MEPs represent the Union's citizens (Art 10(2), 14(2) TEU) and sit by political group, not by nationality. Their mandate is free: they vote on an individual and personal basis, are not bound by instructions and receive no binding mandate (Art 6(1) of the 1976 Act on the election of MEPs). Groups exert political pressure, but there is no enforceable group discipline.
• (b) False. Under the EP Rules of Procedure a group needs at least 23 Members elected in at least one quarter of the Member States (7 of 27), and no one may belong to more than one group. European political parties are a different thing (Art 10(4) TEU, Art 224 TFEU).
• (c) False. Since the 2004 elections, membership of the EP is incompatible with membership of a national parliament (Art 7(2) of the 1976 Act), and also with being a member of a national government or of the Commission (Art 7(1)).
• (d) False. The institutions' seats are fixed by common accord of the Member States' governments (Art 341 TFEU). Protocol No 6: the EP's seat is Strasbourg, where the twelve monthly plenary sessions, including the budget session, are held; additional sessions and committee meetings take place in Brussels, and the General Secretariat is in Luxembourg. The EP cannot change this itself (France v Parliament, C-345/95).
• Also: the EP acts by a majority of the votes cast unless the Treaties provide otherwise (Art 231 TFEU); its Rules of Procedure set the quorum (one third of Members); it elects its President and officers from among its Members (Art 14(4) TEU), the President for two and a half years under its Rules of Procedure.
Codex: Art 10, 14 TEU; Art 224, 231, 232, 341 TFEU; Protocol No 6 · 1976 Act on the election of MEPs and EP Rules of Procedure (not in codex) · France v Parliament (C-345/95).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: A basic regulation on animal-disease control provides that, on duly justified imperative grounds of urgency, Art 8 of Regulation 182/2011 applies; otherwise implementing acts follow the examination procedure. After an outbreak of a cattle disease the Commission immediately bans cattle movements from three regions by implementing act. (a) Was it allowed to act before consulting the comitology committee? (b) Three weeks later the committee delivers a negative opinion by qualified majority. What follows? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes, because the basic act provides for the urgency procedure – the act applies immediately, for at most six months; (b) the Commission must repeal the act immediately.
• Normal rule: draft implementing acts are first submitted to a committee of Member State representatives (Art 291(3) TFEU; Regulation 182/2011, Arts 4–5).
• (a) Art 8 Reg 182/2011: only where the basic act so provides, and on duly justified imperative grounds of urgency, the Commission adopts an implementing act that applies immediately without prior submission to a committee. It remains in force for no more than six months unless the basic act provides otherwise (Art 8(2)), and the chair must submit it to the committee at the latest 14 days after adoption (Art 8(3)). Both conditions are met here.
• (b) Where the examination procedure applies and the committee delivers a negative opinion, the Commission must repeal the act immediately (Art 8(4)). Under the advisory procedure it could keep the act. The urgency track buys the Commission speed, not immunity from the committee's veto.
Codex: Art 291(2)–(3) TFEU · Regulation 182/2011, Arts 4, 5, 8 (not in codex).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: The European trade-union and employers' confederations conclude an EU-level framework agreement giving all workers a right to five days of carer's leave a year, and jointly ask for it to be made binding. (a) How can such an agreement become binding Union law? (b) Is the Commission obliged to submit a proposal? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) At the joint request of the signatories, by a Council decision on a Commission proposal (Art 155(2) TFEU), in practice a directive annexing the agreement; (b) no – the Commission has discretion (EPSU v Commission, C-928/19 P).
• Social dialogue: before submitting social-policy proposals the Commission must consult management and labour on the direction and content of Union action (Art 154(2)–(3)); they may instead negotiate themselves, normally for up to nine months (Art 154(4)), which may lead to agreements (Art 155(1)).
• (a) Two ways of implementation (Art 155(2)): autonomously, through the practices of management and labour and the Member States (e.g. telework 2002); or, in matters covered by Art 153, by a Council decision on a Commission proposal at the signatories' joint request – the EP is only informed; QMV, or unanimity where an Art 153(2) unanimity area is touched. Examples: parental leave (Directive 96/34, later 2010/18), part-time work (97/81), fixed-term work (1999/70).
• (b) The Commission keeps its right of initiative and may refuse to propose (EPSU, 2021). The social partners are thus 'co-decision-makers' – one of the lecture's four roles of interest groups, beside lobbying, consultation and supervision.
Codex: Art 17(2) TEU; Art 152–155 TFEU · EPSU v Commission (C-928/19 P).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Ms Sørensen, a Danish citizen living in Vienna, turns to the European Ombudsman with three complaints: (a) the Commission has for ten months ignored her request for access to documents on a trade negotiation; (b) the General Court dismissed her action for annulment by an order she considers wrong; (c) the Vienna municipal authorities mishandled her residence registration under the Citizens' Rights Directive. Which complaints can the Ombudsman examine, and what can the Ombudsman do? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only complaint (a): the Ombudsman investigates maladministration by Union bodies – not the CJEU acting in its judicial role and not national authorities – and can only recommend and report, not annul or order.
• Legal basis and status: Art 228 TFEU, Art 24 TFEU, Art 43 Charter – a body ensuring that the institutions observe good administration (Art 41 Charter), i.e. internal control independent of litigation. Elected by the EP after each election for its term, re-eligible, completely independent; can be dismissed only by the Court of Justice at the EP's request (Art 228(2)–(3)).
• Who may complain: any Union citizen or any natural or legal person residing or having its registered office in a Member State – Ms Sørensen qualifies on both counts.
• (a) Yes: leaving a request unanswered for ten months is maladministration (reasonable time, Art 41(1) Charter; access to documents, Art 15(3) TFEU, Art 42 Charter).
• (b) No: the CJEU acting in its judicial role is excluded; her remedy is an appeal on points of law to the Court of Justice within two months (Art 256(1) TFEU, Art 56 Statute).
• (c) No: the Ombudsman controls only Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. National authorities are for national courts and ombudsmen (in Austria the Volksanwaltschaft), or a complaint to the Commission.
• Powers: inquiries on complaint or on the Ombudsman's own initiative, except where the facts are or have been the subject of legal proceedings. If maladministration is found, the institution has three months to reply; the Ombudsman then reports to the EP and the institution, and submits an annual report to the EP. There are no binding decisions – the control is reputational.
Codex: Art 15(3), 24, 228, 256(1) TFEU; Arts 41–43 Charter; Art 56 Statute.

cards.q: (a) Name three setbacks of European integration between 1954 and 1970. (b) List the enlargements of the Communities/Union with years and acceding states, and say when the Union became smaller. (c) When did Austria join, together with which states, and which state signed the same accession treaty but did not join? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Failure of the European Defence and Political Communities (1954), the founding of the rival EFTA (1960) and the French vetoes of British membership (1963, 1967); (b) 1973, 1981, 1986, 1995, 2004, 2007, 2013, with the UK leaving in 2020; (c) 1 January 1995, with Finland and Sweden – Norway stayed out.
• (a) The EDC treaty (signed 1952) was rejected by the French National Assembly in August 1954, and the European Political Community fell with it; integration then continued through the economy (Messina 1955, Treaties of Rome 1957). In 1960 the UK and six other states, including Austria, founded EFTA as an intergovernmental free-trade alternative. De Gaulle vetoed the British applications in 1963 and 1967, so the UK joined only in 1973. (A further crisis: the 'empty chair' of 1965, ended by the Luxembourg Compromise of 1966.)
• (b) Founders 1957/58: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands (6). 1973: Denmark, Ireland, UK (9). 1981: Greece (10). 1986: Portugal, Spain (12). 1995: Austria, Finland, Sweden (15). 2004: Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia (25). 2007: Bulgaria, Romania (27). 2013: Croatia (28). 31 January 2020: the UK withdrew under Art 50 TEU (27).
• (c) Austria applied in 1989, approved membership in the referendum of 12 June 1994 (about two thirds in favour) and acceded on 1 January 1995 together with Finland and Sweden. Norway signed the same accession treaty but rejected membership in its 1994 referendum.
• Today's candidates include Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia and the Western Balkan states (Kosovo only a potential candidate); Turkey is a candidate without active negotiations.
Codex: Art 49, 50 TEU – dates are not in the codex, learn them.

cards.q: What makes EU law different from classical international law? Name and briefly explain the features that are said to make the Union legal order supranational. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: EU law is an autonomous legal order: it is made largely by majority through the Union method, applies directly in the Member States, can be invoked by individuals, prevails over national law, is enforced by national authorities and courts under EU-set standards, entails state liability and is subject to fundamental-rights review.
• Starting point: Van Gend en Loos (26/62) – 'a new legal order of international law' whose subjects include individuals; Costa v ENEL (6/64) – its own legal system, integrated into the national legal systems. Classical international law binds mainly states, often needs national transformation and depends on consent and reciprocity.
• Union method: the Commission's monopoly of initiative (Art 17(2) TEU), QMV in the Council (Art 16(3) TEU), the EP as co-legislator (Art 294 TFEU) and full judicial control – states can be outvoted and are still bound.
• Autonomy: own concepts and methods of interpretation, protected by the CJEU's exclusive jurisdiction (Art 19(1) TEU; Art 267, 344 TFEU; Opinion 2/13).
• Primacy: any EU law prevails over any conflicting national law (Costa; Simmenthal, 106/77; Declaration 17).
• Direct applicability (e.g. regulations, Art 288(2) TFEU) and direct effect: clear, precise and unconditional provisions can be invoked by individuals before national courts (Van Gend en Loos).
• Decentralised enforcement: by national authorities and courts (Art 4(3), 19(1) second subpara TEU; Art 291(1) TFEU) under procedural autonomy limited by equivalence and effectiveness (Rewe, Comet), with Art 267 as the link.
• Liability and rights: liability of the Union (Art 340(2) TFEU) and of Member States (Francovich, C-6/90), and fundamental-rights protection against both (Art 6 TEU, Charter).
Codex: Art 4(3), 6, 16(3), 17(2), 19(1) TEU; Art 267, 288, 291(1), 294, 340, 344 TFEU; Declaration 17 · Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Costa v ENEL (6/64), Simmenthal (106/77), Francovich (C-6/90), Rewe (33/76), Opinion 2/13.

cards.q: In Member State Polania a new chamber of the Supreme Court is staffed with judges appointed on the proposal of a judicial council that lacks independence, although a national court had suspended the appointments. A judge of that chamber, sitting alone, dismisses by final order the appeal of judge W against his forced transfer. Another chamber of the Supreme Court, seised of W's related application to recuse the judges of that chamber, wonders whether it must respect the order as res judicata or may treat it as null and void. How must it proceed? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It must declare the order null and void where that is essential to ensure the primacy of EU law – legal certainty and finality cannot prevail over the requirement of an independent tribunal established by law (W.Ż., C-487/19).
• Normal rule: primacy requires only that conflicting national law be disapplied, not that it be declared void (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97), and EU law generally respects res judicata (Kapferer, C-234/04).
• But Art 19(1) second subpara TEU, read with Art 47 Charter, requires that courts deciding in fields covered by EU law be independent and impartial tribunals previously established by law. A judge appointed in manifest breach of the fundamental appointment rules, in a way that casts legitimate doubt on his independence, does not form such a tribunal.
• W.Ż. (2021), confirmed in AW 'T' (C-225/22, 2025) for decisions of the Polish Chamber of Extraordinary Control: no consideration of legal certainty or finality prevents the national court from declaring such a decision null and void where that is essential in the procedural situation to guarantee primacy. This qualifies the 'disapply, do not annul' rule in extreme rule-of-law situations.
Codex: Art 2, 19(1) TEU; Art 47 Charter · W.Ż. (C-487/19), AW 'T' (C-225/22), IN.CO.GE.'90 (C-10/97), Kapferer (C-234/04).
